chief_complaint: intermittent RUQ pain radiating to back after fatty food
hpi_details: A 26-year-old female presents to the clinic with several episodes of intermittent, cramping right upper quadrant pain radiating to the back, typically triggered by fatty meals and resolving spontaneously within a few hours.
ideas: She thinks she might have developed a stomach ulcer or a sudden food intolerance to fatty foods.
concerns: She is worried that these recurring stomach attacks are an early sign of stomach cancer, which her grandmother died from.
expectations: She hopes to get an ultrasound scan of her stomach to rule out cancer and medication to stop the cramping spasms after dinner.

investigation_events.title: Biliary colic results
investigation_events.availability_message: The biliary laboratory and ultrasound results are now available.

results.value: Multiple mobile gallstones without gallbladder wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid, or sonographic Murphy sign; common bile duct 4 mm

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Biliary Colic is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes dietary fat restriction, analgesia for acute episodes, and elective outpatient laparoscopic cholecystectomy for recurrent symptomatic gallstones, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: intermittent RUQ pain radiating to back after fatty food

Key HPI features: A 26-year-old female presents to the clinic with several episodes of intermittent, cramping right upper quadrant pain radiating to the back, typically triggered by fatty meals and resolving spontaneously within a few hours.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: Temp 36.9C, HR 84, BP 118/74. Mild RUQ tenderness during episodes without rebound, guarding, or a positive Murphy's sign; abdomen soft and non-tender between episodes. Labs: LFTs, amylase, and lipase within normal limits. RUQ ultrasound shows gallstones without gallbladder wall thickening or pericholecystic fluid.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Biliary Colic.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Acute cholecystitis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Pain lasting over 6 hours or fever — suggests cholecystitis instead.
management_principles: Advise a low-fat diet and provide analgesia for acute episodes
Refer for elective outpatient laparoscopic cholecystectomy given recurrent symptomatic gallstones
Provide return precautions for fever, jaundice, or pain lasting beyond a few hours, which would suggest acute cholecystitis or choledocholithiasis
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.objective: Vitals: Temp 36.9C, HR 84, BP 118/74. reference_soap.assessment: Biliary colic due to cholelithiasis, with no sonographic evidence of acute cholecystitis.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Biliary Colic
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Biliary Colic
Implement evidence-based management plan: Low-fat diet, elective outpatient laparoscopic cholecystectomy

teaching.one_liner: A gallstone temporarily blocks the cystic duct, causing intermittent RUQ pain radiating to the back after fatty food, which resolves once the stone moves.
red_flags: Pain lasting over 6 hours or fever — suggests cholecystitis instead

must_ask.say: Does the pain come on after fatty meals?
Does it radiate to your back?
Does the pain go away on its own after a while?
Have you had any fever with these episodes?

history.answer: I've been getting this bad cramping pain in my upper right belly, especially after I eat greasy or fatty meals.
It first started about three weeks ago, usually coming on about thirty minutes to an hour after having dinner.
The pain is right under my ribs on the right side, and it stays right there without moving anywhere else.
Yes, it shoots straight through to my mid-back and around my right shoulder blade.
It feels like a deep, heavy cramping and squeezing ache that builds up and stays intense.
At its worst, I would rate it around a seven out of ten.
Each attack lasts about two to three hours and then gradually eases up until it goes away completely.
I have had four separate episodes over the past three weeks.
It definitely flares up after eating heavy, fatty foods like fried chicken, pork belly, or cheesy pizza.
Lying down quietly and waiting it out helps, but nothing takes it away immediately.
I had never experienced anything like this until this recent problem started three weeks ago.
Last night I ate fried chicken with one glass of beer, and the pain hit me shortly after.
I feel pretty nauseated when the pain peaks, but I have not vomited at all.
My bowel movements have been completely normal and brown, with no diarrhea, constipation, or pale stools.
No, I have not had any fever, chills, or shivering spells.
No, my eyes and skin look their normal color, and my urine has not looked dark like tea.
I do not have any burning when I pee, no blood in my urine, and no need to urinate more often.
No, I have not felt lightheaded, faint, or dizzy.
No, I do not have any unusual discharge or bleeding between my periods.
No, I do not have any chest pain, heart racing, or shortness of breath.
I haven't taken any pain relievers, aspirin, or anti-inflammatory drugs because the pain usually fades on its own.
No, I have never had irregular heartbeats, heart problems, or blood vessel issues.
I thought I might have an ulcer or maybe developed a new intolerance to fatty foods.
My grandmother died of stomach cancer, so I'm terrified these recurring cramps might be a tumor growing inside me.
I'm hoping you can order a scan to rule out anything serious like cancer and give me medicine to stop the spasms after I eat.
I have no chronic medical conditions, no high blood pressure, and no diabetes.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I am not taking any prescription medications, over-the-counter pills, or dietary supplements.
I have no known allergies to any medicines.
I do not smoke and have never smoked in my life.
I only drink socially, maybe one drink once or twice a month.
I work as an office administrator and live in an apartment with my sister.
My parents and siblings are healthy, and there is no family history of gallbladder or liver trouble.
My last period started two weeks ago, and my cycles come regularly every twenty-eight days.
I am not pregnant, and my partner and I consistently use condoms.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, pulse 84 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, body temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Conjunctivae are pink without pallor, and sclerae are white and anicteric.
Abdomen is flat and symmetrical, without distension, skin lesions, or surgical scars.
Normal active bowel sounds heard across all four quadrants with no abdominal bruits.
Abdomen is resonant to percussion throughout, with no shifting dullness or organomegaly.
Soft abdomen with mild focal tenderness in the right upper quadrant; no guarding or rigidity.
No rebound tenderness in the right upper quadrant or any other abdominal region.
Murphy sign is negative, with no arrest of inspiration upon deep subcostal palpation.
McBurney point is non-tender, and Rovsing, psoas, and obturator signs are negative.
No tenderness to percussion over the bilateral costovertebral angles.
